tests.test: Engine's analog model: next-month density against the long-run average
Engine's analog model: nearest windows against random windows (placebo)
Absorption-ratio jump: a 10% fall within 12 months
Loop persistence jump: a 10% fall within 12 months

findings: The decision engine's new geometric-analog model, which reads next month from the 8 past 36-month windows whose stock-bond covariance is nearest today's, beats the long-run average's predictive log score by 0.031 a month (t 4.0, walked forward since 1940). The placebo says why: 8 windows drawn at random gain 0.032 (t 7.1) and the 8 farthest 0.010. Most of the gain is mixing several past years, which fattens the tails a single normal misses; the geometry itself adds -0.0009 over random (t -0.2) and +0.021 over the farthest (t 1.9).

As a point forecast the same geometry fails: covariance analogs forecast the next year's stock return with skill -14% against the historical mean (t -2.1) and its volatility with -12% against trailing volatility (t -1.0); matching whole distributions (sliced Wasserstein) gives -27% (t -2.6). Eight neighbours are too few to average out what the next year does, so the engine uses analogs for spread and keeps their means shrunk hard toward the long run.

Today's three-asset structure (stocks 11% volatility, Treasuries 6%, gold 15%, stock-bond correlation +0.25) sits nearest 1972-09, 1985-11, 2000-06, 1977-11; the year after those windows returned +3.6% on average against +8.8% for every month, a spread the tests above say not to trade on.
Of six eras, today's covariance is closest to the Frechet mean of 1973-1999 (distance 0.41, against 7.8 for the farthest): the era of floating gold and stocks and bonds that fell together.

Random matrix theory on 27 monthly series over the last ten years: 2 eigenvalues rise above the Marchenko-Pastur noise edge of 2.17, so the world's markets carry about 2 real common factors and the rest is noise of a finite sample; factor 1 (41% of the variance) loads most on SGD, NZD, AUD; factor 2 (14% of the variance) loads most on WTI, Brent, 10-year. After the absorption ratio jumped, a 10% fall followed within a year 32% of the time against 22% otherwise (block-permutation p 0.29).
Persistent homology of the same geometry: after loops grew unusually persistent, a 10% fall followed 35% of the time against 19% (p 0.15), suggestive on 26 months but not evidence.

Monthly real stock returns have a Hurst exponent of 0.69 against 0.51 to 0.59 for the same months shuffled; much of that is Shiller's monthly-average prices, which smooth returns (first-month autocorrelation +0.26 over the whole sample, +0.18 since 1990).
Of 8 geometric claims tested, 1 survives a 10% false-discovery rate: engine's analog model: next-month density against the long-run average.
